{{(\langle{\text{{*}}\mathtt{E}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\mathtt{F}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}}

and

{{(\langle{\text{{*}}\mathtt{E}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\mathtt{F}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}}

under the layouts
w_{1}
and
w_{2}
respectively, obtaining:

{{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},{w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime}[{p}\leftarrow{v}]})}}

and

{{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},{w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime}[{p}\leftarrow{v}]})}}.

Since
p\in\underline{w}_{1}(\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{u}})

and by definition of
\underline{w}_{1}
, we deduce that
there exist
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}}\in\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{u}}

and
0\leq i\leq\mathsf{size}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}})
such that
w_{1}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}})+i=p
.
By (†), we also deduce that
w_{2}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}})+i=p
,
so we can apply
Remark

4

in order to show that:

{w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime}[{p}\leftarrow{v}]}=w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}[{({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}},i)}\leftarrow{v}]}

and that

{w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime}[{p}\leftarrow{v}]}=w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}[{({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}},i)}\leftarrow{v}]}.

Finally, since
\mathtt{u}({\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime}})
holds
and we have:

{\tau^{\prime}[{({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}},i)}\leftarrow{v}]}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}{\tau^{\prime}}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau,

we can apply the IH, and conclude the proof of this
sub-derivation.

-

Case

p\notin P
. In this case,
from (†), we deduce that

p\notin\underline{w}_{2}(\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{u}})
. Therefore, the
rule
applies, showing both:

w_{1}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\text{{*}}\mathtt{E}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\mathtt{F}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to\mathsf{err},

and

w_{2}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\text{{*}}\mathtt{E}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\mathtt{F}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to\mathsf{err}.

This establishes the claim.

-

Case

x\ \mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}\text{{*}}{\mathtt{E}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D}
. Analogous to the
case of memory store operations.

-

Case

{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{call}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\mathtt{F}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{F}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D}
. This case is also similar to that of memory loads,
but requires some non-trivial observations. As before, we
define
p=\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w_{1}}^{\mathsf{Addr}}
and observe
that
p=\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w_{2}}^{\mathsf{Addr}}
because of

Remark

3
. Similarly, we introduce the values

v_{1},\dots,v_{k}
which correspond to the semantics of

\mathtt{F}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{F}_{k}
evaluated under
\rho
and both
layouts
w_{1},w_{2}
. By (†), we have

w_{1}(\mathsf{ProcId}_{\mathtt{u}})=w_{2}(\mathsf{ProcId}_{\mathtt{u}})
, so we denote this set

P_{\mathsf{ProcId}_{\mathtt{u}}}
, and we go by case analysis on

p\in P_{\mathsf{ProcId}_{\mathtt{u}}}
.

-

Case

p\in P_{\mathsf{ProcId}_{\mathtt{u}}}
. In this case, there exists

{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}}\in\mathsf{ProcId}_{\mathtt{u}}
such that
w_{1}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})=p
, and from
(†) we deduce
p=w_{2}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})
. Using these intermediate
conclusions and the definition of
\mathrel{\diamond}
, we deduce that

(w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})(p)=\tau^{\prime}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})=\tau({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})
, (the
last step follows from the assumption
\tau^{\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau
),
and similarly for
w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime}(p)
. Since

p\in P_{\mathsf{ProcId}_{\mathtt{u}}}
, we deduce that rule
can
be applied, proving:

w_{1}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{call}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\mathtt{F}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{F}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to\\
{{(\langle\tau({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{u}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}},

and

w_{2}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{call}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\mathtt{F}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{F}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to\\
{{(\langle\tau({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{u}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}},

where
\rho_{0}^{\prime}=\rho_{0}[x_{1},\dots,x_{k}\leftarrow v_{1},\dots,v_{k}]
.
Finally, by assumption on
\tau
, we know that
\tau({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})
is an unprivileged program. So, in particular,

\mathtt{u}({\langle\tau({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{u}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime}})

holds. This allows us to apply the IH and conclude the proof.

-

Case

p\notin P_{\mathsf{ProcId}_{\mathtt{u}}}
. Analogous to the corresponding case for store operations.

-

Case

{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{E}_{1},\ldots,\mathtt{E}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D}
. This is perhaps the most interesting
case of this proof. We begin by introducing the values

v_{1},\dots,v_{k}
, which correspond to the
semantics of
\mathtt{F}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{F}_{k}
evaluated under

\rho
as well as any of layouts
w_{1},w_{2}
.These
values do not depend on the layout because of
Remark

3
. By
introspection of the rule
, we deduce that
both the following statements hold:

w_{1}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{F}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{F}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to\\
{{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}},

and

w_{2}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{F}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{F}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to\\
{{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}},

where

\rho_{0}^{\prime}=\rho_{0}[x_{1},\dots,x_{k}\leftarrow v_{1},\dots,v_{k}]
. Unfortunately, we cannot apply the IH
to the configuration

{{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}}

because
\mathtt{u}(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime})
does not hold. However, we can go by cases on

\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w_{1}}({{\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}})},{\rho_{0}^{\prime}},{\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}},\tau^{\prime}})

-

Case

\Omega
. By
Lemma

10
, we deduce that

\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w_{1}}({(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})})=\Omega,

which leads to a contradiction because we assumed

w_{1}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{n+1}\phi_{1}\land w_{1}\vdash_{\sigma}\phi_{1}{\downarrow}_{.}

-

Case

\mathsf{unsafe}
. From the
layout non-intreference property
(
Definition

2
), we deduce that

\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w_{2}}({\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}},\tau^{\prime}})\in\{\mathsf{err},\mathsf{unsafe}\}.

We take
\mathsf{err}
as an example. This means that

\exists h.w_{2}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle,w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{h}\mathsf{err}.

By applying
Lemma

10
to the reduction with
w_{1}
,
we deduce that

w_{1}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{n}\mathsf{unsafe}.

By applying
Lemma

10
to the
reduction with
w_{2}
, we deduce that:

w_{2}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},b\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!}\mathsf{err}.

We conclude by observing that
\mathsf{unsafe}\cong\mathsf{err}
. The case with
\mathsf{unsafe}
follows analogously.

-

Case

\mathsf{err}
. Analogous to the previous case.

-

Case

(v,m)
.
We start by observing that
m=w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime}
for some
\tau^{\prime\prime}
due to
Remark

5
. Form the
layout non-interference

property (
Definition

2
),
we deduce that

\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w_{2}}({\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}})},{\rho_{0}^{\prime}},{\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}},\tau^{\prime})={(v,\tau^{\prime\prime})}.

By applying
Lemma

10
twice, we deduce that:

w_{1}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{F}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{F}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to\\
{{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}}\to^{*}\\
{{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{\mathit{ret}}\leftarrow{v}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})}}

and

w_{2}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{F}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{F}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to\\
{{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}}\to^{*}\\
{{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{\mathit{ret}}\leftarrow{v}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})}}

Next, we observe that we assumed

w_{1}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{F}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{F}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{n+1}{\phi_{1}},

and
\phi_{1}
is terminal, so it must be the case that

w_{1}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{\mathit{ret}}\leftarrow{v}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})}\to^{!}\phi_{1}
. In particular, the
reduction requires less than
n+1
steps. From the
assumption
\mathtt{u}(F)
, we also deduce
\mathtt{u}(F^{\prime})
, and

\mathtt{u}(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{\mathit{ret}}\leftarrow{v}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime})
and
from
Remark

5
we conclude that

\tau^{\prime\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau^{\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau
, so we can apply the IH
to

{{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{\mathit{ret}}\leftarrow{v}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{1}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})}}

and deduce that

\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w_{2}}({(\langle\varepsilon,\rho^{\prime},b_{2}\rangle:F^{\prime},w_{2}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})})\cong\phi_{1},

which concludes the proof.

∎

Lemma 8

(Main Lemma)
.

Let
\sigma=(\tau,\gamma,\xi)
be a
layout non-interferent
system.
For every
n\in\mathbb{N}
,

unprivileged
program
\mathtt{C}
,
register map
\rho
, and distribution
\mu
,
if

\forall w\in\mathsf{Layout}.\exists\chi_{w}.w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{!n}\chi_{w},

then one of the two following statements must hold:

–

There are a register map
\rho^{\prime}
and a store
\tau^{\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau

such that, for every layout
w
, we have the reduction

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{!n}{(\langle\varepsilon,\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{u}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}.

–

\Pr_{w\leftarrow\mu}\left[w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{!n}\mathsf{err}\right]\geq\delta_{\mu}.

Proof.

To facilitate the induction, we prove a slightly stronger statement. Specifically, we replace the quantification over
\mathtt{C}
and
\rho
with a quantification over a non-empty stack
F
such that
\mathtt{u}(F)
holds. Additionally, we quantify over a general
\tau^{\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau
instead of
\tau
, and we rewrite the claim in a more convenient form. In the following claim, all meta-variables that are not explicitly quantified are globally and universally quantified. As a result, we obtain the following claim:
if
\forall w\in\mathsf{Layout}.\exists\chi_{w}.w\vdash_{\sigma}{(F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!n}\chi_{w}
, then:

–

\exists\rho^{\prime},\tau^{\prime\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau^{\prime}.\forall w\in\mathsf{Layout}.w\vdash_{\sigma}{(F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!n}{{(\langle\varepsilon,\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{u}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})}}
, or

–

\Pr_{w\leftarrow\mu}\left[w\vdash_{\sigma}{(F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!n}\mathsf{err}\right]\geq\delta_{\mu}
.

We call this auxiliary claim (C’) and we proceed by induction on
n
.

-

Case
0. In this case, we assume

\forall w\in\mathsf{Layout}.\exists\chi_{w}.w\vdash_{\sigma}{(F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!0}\chi_{w},

and from this premise, we deduce that

{(F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}
is terminal. Using the definition
of the notation
\to^{!}
, the fact that
\mathtt{u}(F)
holds, and the
assumption on the non-emptiness of
F
, we conclude that

F=\langle\varepsilon,\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:\epsilon
for some
\rho
. Hence, the claim
holds trivially by choosing the register map
\rho
and the
store
\tau^{\prime}
.

-

Case

n+1
. In this case, we start by assuming

\forall w\in\mathsf{Layout}.\exists\chi_{w}.w\vdash_{\sigma}{(F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!n+1}\chi_{w}

and we go by cases on
F
, excluding the case where
F=\epsilon
due to our assumption on the non-emptiness of
F
.
Therefore, in the following, we assume that
F=\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime}
,
and we proceed by cases on
\mathtt{C}
. Notice that the induction
hypothesis coincides syntactically with (C’).

-

Case

x\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}\mathtt{E}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D}
. In this case, we observe
that there exists a value
v
such that, for every layout

w
, we have
\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}=v
. More
specifically, this follows from
Remark

3
, since for
every
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}\in\mathsf{Id}_{\mathtt{u}}
and every pair of layouts
w_{1},w_{2}
,
it holds that
w_{1}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}})=w_{2}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}})
. In particular, all
identifiers appearing in
\mathtt{E}
belong to
\mathsf{Id}_{\mathtt{u}}
.
By introspection of the semantics, we deduce that for every layout
w
:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle x\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}\mathtt{E}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to\\
{{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{x}\leftarrow{v}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}}.

(
*
)

Notice that

\mathtt{u}(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{x}\leftarrow{v}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime})
. Because of (H) and this observation, we
can apply the IH to the stack in the target configuration and

\tau^{\prime}
to conclude that one among (A) and (B) below holds.

\exists\rho^{\prime},\tau^{\prime\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau^{\prime}.\forall w\in\mathsf{Layout}.\\
w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{x}\leftarrow{v}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!n}\\
{{(\langle\varepsilon,\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{u}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})}}

(A)

\Pr_{w\leftarrow\mu}\left[w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{x}\leftarrow{v}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!n}\mathsf{err}\right]\geq\delta_{\mu}.

We go by cases on this disjunction.

-

Case
A. In this case, we introduce
\rho^{\prime}
and
\tau^{\prime\prime}
from the IH,
we assume
\tau^{\prime\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau^{\prime}
, we fix a layout
w
and from
(
*
) and (A), we conclude:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle x\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}\mathtt{E}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{n+1}{{(\langle\varepsilon,\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{u}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})}}.

Due to the generality of
w
, we can
introduce universal quantification over all layouts, thereby
completing the proof.

-

Case
B. We call
E
the set of all the layouts
\overline{w}
such that

\overline{w}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{x}\leftarrow{v}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!n}\mathsf{err}

Notice that we can apply the assumption (
*
)
to each of these layouts, showing that

\forall\overline{w}\in E.\overline{w}\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle x\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}\mathtt{E}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},\overline{w}\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!n+1}\mathsf{err}.

From (B), we know that the probability associated to the event
E
is bigger than
\delta_{\mu}
,
the last observation establishes the claim.

-

Case

\varepsilon
. Analogous to the previous case.

-

Case

{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{skip}}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D}
. Analogous to the case of
assignments.

-

Case

{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{if}}}\ \mathtt{E}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{then}}}\ \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}\mathtt{C}_{\bot}\end{array}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{else}}}\ \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}\mathtt{C}_{\top}\end{array}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{fi}}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D}
.
Analogous to the case of assignments.

-

Case

{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{while}}}\ \mathtt{E}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{do}}}\ \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}\mathtt{C}\end{array}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{od}}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D}

-

Case

{\text{{*}}\mathtt{E}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\mathtt{F}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D}
. In this case,
we begin by observing that there exists a value
v_{\mathtt{E}}

such that for every

, we have

. This follows from

3
, since we assume that

\mathtt{u}({\text{{*}}\mathtt{E}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\mathtt{F}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D})

all identifiers within

\mathsf{Id}_{\mathtt{u}}

For the same reason, there exists a unique value
v_{\mathtt{F}}

w

\llbracket\mathtt{F}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}=v_{\mathtt{F}}

there is a unique address
p\in\mathsf{Addr}

p=v^{\mathsf{Addr}}

Similarly, we deduce that there exists a unique set of addresses

such that, for every layout
w

\underline{w}(\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{u}})=P_{\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{u}}}
. Moreover, due to the
assumptions on the set of layouts, we conclude that

Finally, we proceed by cases on whether

-

Case

p\in P_{\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{u}}}
. The rule

can be applied to each configuration

{{(\langle{\text{{*}}\mathtt{E}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\mathtt{F}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}}

for every layout

{{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},{w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime}[{p}\leftarrow{v_{\mathtt{E}}}]})}};

from the assumption

and the definition of
\underline{w}
, we deduce that
there is
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}}\in\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{u}}

and
0\leq i\leq\mathsf{size}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}})

and that for every other layout

it must hold that
\overline{w}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}})+i=p
,
so we can apply
Remark

4

in order to show that

\forall w\in\mathsf{Layout}.{w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime}[{p}\leftarrow{v_{\mathtt{E}}}]}=w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}[{({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}},i)}\leftarrow{v_{\mathtt{E}}}]}.

Finally, we observe that
\mathtt{u}({\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime}})
holds
and that

{\tau^{\prime}[{({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}},i)}\leftarrow{v_{\mathtt{E}}}]}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}{\tau^{\prime}}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau

holds as well, so we can apply the IH
and conclude the proof of this sub-derivation as we did in the case of assignments.

-

p\notin P_{\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{u}}}

In this case,
we just observe that
the rule

This establishes the claim.

-

10
, we conclude that

{{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{\mathit{ret}}\leftarrow{\overline{\rho}(\mathit{ret})}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\overline{\tau})}}.

From (B), we know that the probability measure associated with

, we deduce that

\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w}({(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})})=\Omega,

The main claim is a particular case of C’ where

is
\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle
, and

is
\tau
.

See
2

Proof.

We begin by fixing all the universally quantified variables in the
statement using the same meta-variable as before. We also fix some

\overline{w}\in\mathsf{Layout}
and proceed by case analysis on

\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,\overline{w}}({(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}).

-

Case

(v,\tau^{\prime\prime})
.
In this case, by the
layout non-interference
property, we conclude that (A) holds for
\overline{v}=v
and
\overline{\tau}=\tau^{\prime\prime}
. Furthermore, by

\tau^{\prime\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau^{\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau
.

-

Case

\mathsf{unsafe},\mathsf{err}
.
Here, by the
layout non-interference
property, we deduce that for every
w\in\mathsf{Layout}
,

\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w}({(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})})\in\{\mathsf{err},\mathsf{unsafe}\}.

Consequently, for every
w\in\mathsf{Layout}
, there exists some
n_{w}
such that

\exists n_{w}.w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{n_{w}}\chi\in\{\mathsf{err},\mathsf{unsafe}\}.

Since
\mathsf{Layout}
is finite, there exists a uniform bound
\overline{n}
such that

\forall w\in\mathsf{Layout}.w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!\overline{n}}\chi\in\{\mathsf{err},\mathsf{unsafe}\}.

From this, we conclude that

\Pr_{w\leftarrow\mu}\left[w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!\overline{n}}\mathsf{err}\right]\geq\delta_{\mu}.

This follows by considering an enumeration
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{0},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{h}
of the identifiers in
\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}))
and noting that the probability above can be rewritten as:

\sum_{p_{1},\dots,p_{h}\in\mathsf{Addr}_{\mathtt{k}}}\Pr_{w\leftarrow\mu}\Big[w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!\overline{n}}\mathsf{err}\,\,\Big|\,\,\forall 1\leq i\leq h.w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{i})=p_{i}\Big]\cdot\\
\Pr_{w\leftarrow\mu}[w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{1})=p_{1},\dots,w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{h})=p_{h}]

From (†) and
Lemma

1
, we deduce that for every
choice of
p_{1},\dots,p_{h}\in\mathsf{Addr}_{\mathtt{k}}
, the terms on the left
in the expression above are bounded by
\delta_{\mu}
making
their convex combination bounded by
\delta_{\mu}
. moreover, since:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!\overline{n}}\mathsf{err}\Rightarrow w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!}\mathsf{err}

for the definition of
\to^{!m}
, and this means that

\Pr_{w\leftarrow\mu}\left[w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!}\mathsf{err}\right]\geq\Pr_{w\leftarrow\mu}\left[w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{!\overline{n}}\mathsf{err}\right],

which establishes the claim.

-

Case

\Omega
. In this case, due to the
layout non-interference
property, we conclude that (C) holds.

∎

For the next lemma, we extend
\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}
to frame stacks as follows:

\displaystyle\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(\epsilon)

\displaystyle\triangleq\emptyset

\displaystyle\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(f\mathrel{:}F)

\displaystyle\triangleq\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(f)\cup\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(F)

\displaystyle\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle)

-

w_{1},w_{2}

w_{1}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}})=w_{2}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}})
. In
particular, this applies to identifiers appearing in
\mathtt{E}

that belong to
\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}))
by (H). For all
layouts if our quantification layouts, we have:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle x\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}\mathtt{E}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})}\to\\
{{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho^{\prime}[{x}\leftarrow{v}]},\mathtt{k}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})}}.

(
*
)

From (H), we deduce

\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho^{\prime}[{x}\leftarrow{v}]},\mathtt{k}\rangle:F^{\prime})\subseteq\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}))

Therefore, we conclude that (A) holds if either

\mathtt{D}\neq\varepsilon
or
F^{\prime}
is non-empty. Otherwise, (C)
holds.

is greater than

Remark 2
.

\delta_{\nu}\geq\min_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}\in\mathsf{Sys}}\frac{\kappa_{\mathtt{k}}/\theta-|{\mathsf{Id}_{\mathtt{k}}}|}{\kappa_{\mathtt{k}}/\theta-|{\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}))\setminus\mathsf{Sys}}|}

Proof.

We want to prove that

\min\bigl\{\displaystyle{\Pr_{w\leftarrow\nu}}[p\notin\underline{w}(\mathsf{Id})\mid w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{i}^{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}})=p_{i},\text{ for }1\leq i\leq h]\mid{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}\in\mathsf{Sys},p,p_{1},\dots,p_{h}\in\mathsf{Addr}_{\mathtt{k}}\land{}\\[3.0pt]
\phantom{{}\mid}p\notin\{p_{i},\ldots,p_{i}+\mathsf{size}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{i}^{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}})-1\},\text{ for }1\leq i\leq h\bigr\}.

is greater than

\min_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}\in\mathsf{Sys}}\frac{\kappa_{\mathtt{k}}/\theta-|{\mathsf{Id}_{\mathtt{k}}}|}{\kappa_{\mathtt{k}}/\theta-|{\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}))}\setminus\mathsf{Sys}|}
.
To establish this, we fix a system call
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}\in\mathsf{Sys}

and addresses

p,p_{1},\dots,p_{h}\in\mathsf{Addr}_{\mathtt{k}}
that achieve the minimum.
In particular, we have:

p\notin\{p_{i},\ldots,p_{i}+\mathsf{size}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{i}^{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}})-1\},\text{ for }1\leq i\leq h.

Given that the minimum exists,
p_{1},\ldots,p_{h}
are the starting
addresses of the slots
s_{1},\ldots,s_{h}
where the references

\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}))\setminus\mathsf{Sys}
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}
are allocated.
Now, assume that
p
is located within one of these slots, say

s_{j}
. From assumption (†), we deduce that
p
cannot be
allocated, since no object other than
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{j}
can be placed in that
slot. As a result, we obtain:

\Pr_{w\leftarrow\nu}[p\notin\underline{w}(\mathsf{Id})\mid w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{i}^{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}})=p_{i},\text{ for }1\leq i\leq h]=1,

which establishes the claim.

If, on the other hand,
p
is located in a different slot
s
, we observe that:

\Pr_{w\leftarrow\nu}[p\notin\underline{w}(\mathsf{Id})\mid w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{i}^{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}})=p_{i},\text{ for }1\leq i\leq h]\geq\\
\Pr_{w\leftarrow\nu}[\mathit{slotof}(p)\notin w(\mathsf{Id})\mid w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{i}^{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}})=p_{i},\text{ for }1\leq i\leq h]

where
\mathit{slotof}
associates each address with the starting
address of its corresponding slot.
Due to the definition of
\nu
, the slots are sampled uniformly and
they are independent. Therefore, the probability to the right in
(
*
) is given by the ratio of the free slots and those that are not
occupied by elements of

\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}))\setminus\mathsf{Sys}
, because of the
assumption (†). In conclusion (
*
) is equal to:

\frac{\kappa_{\mathtt{k}}/\theta-|{\mathsf{Id}_{\mathtt{k}}}|}{\kappa_{\mathtt{k}}/\theta-|{\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}))}\setminus\mathsf{Sys}|}\geq\min_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}\in\mathsf{Sys}}\frac{\kappa_{\mathtt{k}}/\theta-|{\mathsf{Id}_{\mathtt{k}}}|}{\kappa_{\mathtt{k}}/\theta-|{\mathsf{refs}_{\sigma}(\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}))}\setminus\mathsf{Sys}|}.

∎

Technical observations

Remark 3
.

Let
\{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{1},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{h}\}\subseteq\mathsf{Id}
be a set of identifiers,
\{p_{1},\dots,p_{h}\}
a set of addresses, and
W\subseteq\{w\in\mathsf{Layout}\mid\forall 1\leq i\leq h,\,w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{i})=p_{i}\}
a set of layouts. Given an expression
\mathtt{E}
such that
\mathsf{ids}(\mathtt{E})\subseteq\{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{1},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{h}\}
and a register map
\rho
, there exists a value
v\in\mathsf{Val}
such that

\forall w\in W,\,\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}=v.

Proof.

We proceed by cases on the size of
W
. If
|W|=0
or
|W|=1
, the claim is trivial. Otherwise, we prove the following auxiliary claim:

\forall\mathtt{E}.\mathsf{ids}(\mathtt{E})\subseteq\{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{1},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{h}\}\Rightarrow\forall w_{1},w_{2}\in\mathsf{Layout}.\forall 1\leq i\leq h.w_{1}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{i})=w_{2}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{id}}}_{i})\Rightarrow\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w_{1}}=\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w_{2}},

which can be proved by induction on the syntax of
\mathtt{E}
. The main claim follows from the IH on
W\setminus\{w\}
for some layout
w
, the application of the auxiliary claim to a pair of layouts
\overline{w}\in W\setminus\{w\}
and
w
, and the transitivity of equality.
∎

Remark 4
.

Let
p\in\mathsf{Addr}
be an address,
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}}\in{\mathsf{Arr}}
be an array, and
\tau
be a store. For
0\leq i<\mathsf{size}((){\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}})
, if
p=w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}})+i
, then

{(w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)[{p}\leftarrow{v}]}=w\mathrel{\diamond}({{\tau}[{(p,i)}\leftarrow{v}]}).

Proof.

The claim follows directly from unrolling the definitions.
∎

Remark 5
.

For every layout
w\in\mathsf{Layout}
, and pair of configurations
{(F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}
and
{(F^{\prime},m)}
such that
w\vdash_{\sigma}{(F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{*}{(F^{\prime},m)}
, it holds that
m=w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime}
for some
\tau^{\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau
.

Proof.

The proof proceeds by induction on the length of the reduction. The base case follows from the reflexivity of
=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}
. The inductive case follows from introspection of the rule that has been used for the last transition. The only non-trivial case occurs for the
rule, where the premise
p\in\underline{w}(\mathsf{ArrId}_{b})
guarantees the existence of a pair
({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}},i)
such that
0\leq i<\mathsf{size}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}})
. The observation follows from
Remark

4
.
∎

Lemma 9
.

For every layout
w\in\mathsf{Layout}
, configuration
{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle,m)}
and non-empty stack
f:F
,
n\in\mathbb{N}
, and configuration
\phi
:

–

if
w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{n}{(F^{\prime},m^{\prime})}
, then:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:f:F,m)}\to^{n}{(F^{\prime}:f:F,m^{\prime})}

–

if
w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{n}\mathsf{err}
, then:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:f:F,m)}\to^{n}\mathsf{err}

–

if
w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{n}\mathsf{unsafe}
, then:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:f:F,m)}\to^{n}\mathsf{unsafe}

Proof.

By induction on
n
. The base case is trivial. The inductive
case follows from the IH and by introspection of the rule that
has been used for showing the last transition. In particular, it suffices to
observe that every rule that can be applied to show

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(F^{\prime},m^{\prime})}\to{(F^{\prime\prime},m^{\prime})}

can also be applied to show

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(F^{\prime}:f:F,m^{\prime})}\to{(F^{\prime\prime}:f:F,m^{\prime})}.

∎

Lemma 10
.

For every layout
w\in\mathsf{Layout}
, configuration
{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}
and non-empty stack
\langle\mathtt{D},\rho^{\prime},b\rangle:F
,
n\in\mathbb{N}
, and configuration
\phi
:

–

if
\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w}({(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)})={v,\tau^{\prime}}
, then:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho^{\prime},b\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{*}\\
{{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho^{\prime}[{\mathit{ret}}\leftarrow{v}]},b\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}}

–

if
\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w}({(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)})=\mathsf{err}
, then:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho^{\prime},b\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{*}\mathsf{err}

–

if
\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w}({(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)})=\mathsf{unsafe}
, then:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho^{\prime},b\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{*}\mathsf{unsafe}

–

if
\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w}({(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)})=\Omega
, then:

\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w}({(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho^{\prime},b\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)})=\Omega

Proof.

All cases follow directly from
Lemma

9
. The
first three cases are omitted, as the most interesting one is the
last.
Expanding the definition of
\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w}(\cdot)
, we obtain that
\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w}({(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)})=\Omega
is equivalent to stating that for every
n
,

\exists\chi.w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{n}\chi.

Our goal is to show that for every
n
:

\exists\chi^{\prime}.w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho^{\prime},b\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{n}\chi^{\prime}

Fix
n
. The claim follows by applying (†) to
n
and then using
Lemma

9
on the
n
-step reduction
w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{n}\chi
.
∎

A.2
Appendix for
Section

6

Kernel-mode stack

In this section, the predicate
\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}
additionally requires that all the commands within the stack belong to
\mathtt{Cmd}
, i.e., that they do not contain
{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{spec}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{on}}}\ \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}\cdot\end{array}
,
{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{poison}}}({\cdot})
, and
x\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{observe}}}()
statements:

\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}(\epsilon)\triangleq\top\quad\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}(f:F)\triangleq\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}(f)\land\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}(F)\quad\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle)\triangleq\mathtt{k}(\mathtt{C})\land b=\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\land\mathtt{C}\in\mathtt{Cmd}.

We write
\mathtt{k}(\cdot)
as a shorthand for

\exists{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}\in\mathsf{Sys}.\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}(\cdot)
. Moreover, we relax
the definition of
\mathtt{u}
by not requiring that programs are
unprivileged:

\mathtt{u}(\epsilon)\triangleq\top\quad\mathtt{u}(f:F)\triangleq\mathtt{u}(f)\land\mathtt{u}(F)\quad\mathtt{u}(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle)\triangleq b=\mathtt{u}.

A.2.3
Buffered Memories

Remark 6
.

If
{{({\mu},m)}^{i}}(p)=v,\bot
, then
{{({\mu},m)}^{0}}(p)=v,\bot
.

Proof.

The claim is:

\forall{({\mu},m)}.\forall i.\forall v.{{({\mu},m)}^{i}}(p)=v,\bot\to{{({\mu},m)}^{0}}(p)=v,\bot

We proceed by induction on the length of the buffer
{\mu}
.

-

Case

\epsilon
. The claim follows directly from the definition of lookup.

-

Case

{[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}{\mu}
. By the IH, we have:

\forall i,v.{{({\mu},m)}^{i}}(p)=v,\bot\to{{({\mu},m)}^{i}}(p)={{({\mu},m)}^{0}}(p).

The goal is to prove:

\forall i,v.{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)^{i}}(p)=v,\bot\Rightarrow\\
{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)^{i}}(p)={({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)^{0}}(p).

We proceed by case analysis on
i
.

-

Case

0
. The claim simplifies to:

\forall v.{{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)}^{0}}(p)=v,\bot\Rightarrow\\
{{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)}^{0}}(p)={{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)}^{0}}(p).

The conclusion is trivial.

-

Case

i+1
. The claim now states:

\forall i.\forall v.{{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)}^{i+1}}(p)=v,\bot\Rightarrow\\
{{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)}^{i+1}}(p)={{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)}^{0}}(p).

Fix
i,v
and assume
{{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)}^{i+1}}(p)=v,\bot
, call this assumption (H). The claim simplifies to:

{{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)}^{i+1}}(p)={{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)}^{0}}(p).

Observe that having
p^{\prime}=p
would lead to a contradiction, as (H) and the definition of lookup would imply
\bot=\top
, which is impossible. Hence, we must have
p^{\prime}\neq p
, allowing us to deduce from the definition of lookup that:

\displaystyle{{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)}^{i+1}}(p)

\displaystyle={{({\mu},m)}^{i+1}}(p)

\displaystyle{{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto\overline{v}]}\mathrel{:}\mu,m)}^{0}}(p)

\displaystyle={{({\mu},m)}^{0}}(p)

The claim is a consequence of these equations, the IH and (H).

∎

Remark 7
.

For every buffered memory
{({\mu},m)}
, and every address
p
we have that

{{({\mu},m)}^{0}}(p)=\overline{{({\mu},m)}}(p)
.

Proof.

The proof proceeds by induction on
{\mu}
.

-

Case

{\mu}=\epsilon
. If
{\mu}
is empty, the claim follows
trivially from the definition of lookup.

-

Case

{\mu}={[p^{\prime}\mapsto v]}\mathrel{:}{\mu}
. In this case, the claim states:

{{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto v]}\mathrel{:}{\mu},m)}^{0}}(p)=\overline{{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto v]}\mathrel{:}{\mu},m)}}(p).

Rewriting this proposition, we obtain:

{{({[p^{\prime}\mapsto v]}\mathrel{:}{\mu},m)}^{0}}(p)={\overline{{({\mu},m)}}[{p^{\prime}}\leftarrow{v}]}(p).

Now, we consider two cases:

-

Case

p=p^{\prime}
. In this case, the claim follows directly from the definitions of lookup and memory update.

-

Case

p\neq p^{\prime}
. In this case, the claim follows
from the definition of lookup and the IH.

∎

Remark 8
.

For every buffered memory
{({\mu},(w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau))}

if
\mathsf{dom}({\mu})\subseteq w(\mathsf{ArrId})
,
then we have that:

\overline{{({\mu},(w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau))}}=w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime}

for some
\tau^{\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau

Proof.

The proof is by induction on the length of the buffer.
∎

∎

Lemma 12
.

For every system
\sigma=(\tau,\gamma,\xi)
, and
natural number
n
, configurations

\phi={(\langle\mathtt{C},\overline{\rho},\mathtt{u}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}

with
\tau=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau^{\prime}
and

{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})},

if

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\mathtt{C},\overline{\rho},\mathtt{u}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{n}{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})},

then there exist a configuration

{{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{E}_{1},\ldots,\mathtt{E}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{C},\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime\prime})}},

and a natural number
n^{\prime}<n
such that

w\vdash_{\sigma}\phi\to^{n^{\prime}}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{E}_{1},\ldots,\mathtt{E}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{C},\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime\prime})}\to^{n-n^{\prime}}{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})},

and

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),{\rho_{0}[{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}}\leftarrow{\llbracket\mathtt{E}_{1}\rrbracket_{\rho^{\prime},w},\ldots,\llbracket\mathtt{E}_{k}\rrbracket_{\rho^{\prime},w}}]},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime\prime})}\to^{n-n^{\prime}-1}{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle\mathrel{:}F^{\prime\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})},

where
\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}(F^{\prime\prime})
and
F^{\prime\prime}\mathrel{:}\langle\mathtt{C},\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{u}\rangle\mathrel{:}F^{\prime}=F
.

Proof.

The proof proceeds by induction on
n
. The base case holds
trivially since the premise is vacuous.
For the inductive step, we analyze the last transition using case
analysis on the applied rule.
Most rules follow a uniform argument, except for
and

. We illustrate the proof for the representative
case of rule
, along with the exceptional cases.

-

A.3
Proofs from
Section

8

In this section, the language is extended with the instruction

{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{fence}}}
and with non-speculative call instructions. In order to make
our non-speculative semantics compatible with the extended language,
we enrich the non-speculative semantics of

Figures

3
and
4
with the following rule for the

{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{fence}}}
instruction:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{fence}}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:F,m)}\to{(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:F,m)}

and the following rules for safe calls:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{scall}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\vec{\mathtt{F}}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:F,m)}\to{(\langle m(p),\rho_{0}[\vec{x}\leftarrow\llbracket\vec{\mathtt{F}}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}],b\rangle:\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:F,m)}\lx@proof@logical@and\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}^{\mathsf{Addr}}=pp\in\underline{w}(\mathsf{ProcId}_{b})\framebox{$b=\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\Rightarrow p\in\underline{w}(\xi({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}))$}

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{scall}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\vec{\mathtt{F}}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:F,m)}\to\mathsf{unsafe}\lx@proof@logical@and\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}^{\mathsf{Addr}}=pp\in\underline{w}(\mathsf{ProcId}_{\mathtt{k}})\framebox{$p\not\in\underline{w}(\xi({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}))$}

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{scall}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\vec{\mathtt{F}}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:F,m)}\to\mathsf{err}\lx@proof@logical@and\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}^{\mathsf{Addr}}=pp\notin\underline{w}(\mathsf{ProcId}_{b})

The following remark is useful for the proof of
Theorem

3

Remark 9
.

If
\sigma
is kernel safe,
\zeta
is user-space semantics preserving, and

\zeta(\sigma)=\sigma^{\prime}
, then
\sigma^{\prime}
is also kernel safe.

Proof of
Theorem

3

To aid in proving the upcoming results, we introduce the concept of

well-formedness
for the transformations
\eta
,

{\psi}
, and
\theta
. These relations are designed to
express invariant properties that hold when the execution of a system
call begins and are preserved during kernel-space evaluation. The
corresponding predicates can be found in

Figures

21
,
22
and
23
.

For the well-formedness relation of
{\psi}
in

Figure

22
, we use the auxiliary predicate

\Sigma(\mathtt{C},m,e)
, which holds whenever the command has the form:

\mathtt{C}={\psi^{m}_{e}}(\mathtt{C}^{\prime});{\psi^{\top}_{\bot}}(\mathtt{D}_{1});\ldots;{\psi^{\top}_{\bot}}(\mathtt{D}_{h})
.
In addition, in the rule for configurations, we overload the operator

{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}
to represent the lexical concatenation of two programs
\mathtt{C}

and
\mathtt{D}
, with
\varepsilon
serving as the null element for this
operation. Finally, note that since
k
can be any natural number, we
also account for the case where
\mathtt{D}_{1},\ldots,\mathtt{D}_{k}
is an
empty sequence when
k=0
.

{{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{scall}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\mathtt{E}_{1},\ldots,\mathtt{E}_{n});\mathtt{C}^{\prime},\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:F,\overline{{({\mu}^{\prime\prime},(w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime\prime}))}})}}.

applies to the transition

A.3.1
Technical Observations on the Speculative Semantics

We begin by defining a predicate
\sigma\vdash\mathsf{wf}_{w}(\cdot)
that captures the
well-formedness of a buffered memory with respect to a layout

w
. For a system
\sigma=(\tau,\gamma,\xi)
and a layout

w
, this predicate is defined as follows:

\sigma\vdash\mathsf{wf}_{w}((\mathsf{err},b_{\!\mathit{ms}}))\quad\sigma\vdash\mathsf{wf}_{w}(\mathsf{unsafe})\quad\sigma\vdash\mathsf{wf}_{w}(\epsilon)\quad\sigma\vdash\mathsf{wf}_{w}(\phi:S)\lx@proof@logical@and\sigma\vdash\mathsf{wf}_{w}(\phi)\sigma\vdash\mathsf{wf}_{w}(S)

\sigma\vdash\mathsf{wf}_{w}((F,{({\mu},m)},b_{\!\mathit{ms}}))\lx@proof@logical@and\mathsf{dom}({\mu})\subseteq w(\mathsf{ArrId})m=w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime}\tau^{\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau F=F_{\mathtt{k}}:F_{\mathtt{u}}\mathtt{k}(F_{\mathtt{k}})\mathtt{u}(F_{\mathtt{u}})

Proof.

The proof goes by induction on the number of steps.

-

Case
0. Trivial.

-

Case

n+1
.
The claim is established through a case analysis of the rule used in the last transition. In most cases, the result follows directly from the IH. Therefore, we focus on the most relevant cases.

-

Case

.
Since the target configuration contains a frame stack that is a suffix of the source configuration’s frame stack, the conclusion directly follows from the IH.

-

Case

. The configuration reached after
n
steps can be expressed as follows:

{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{fence}}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,b\rangle:F,{({\mu},w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}})},b_{\!\mathit{ms}})\mathrel{:}S^{\prime\prime}}.

By the IH, we know that this configuration satisfies
\mathsf{wf}
. The target configuration obtained from this step has the following form:

{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,b\rangle:F,{(\epsilon,\overline{{({\mu},w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}})}})},b_{\!\mathit{ms}})\mathrel{:}S^{\prime\prime}}.

The claim then follows from the IH and
Remark

8
.

-

Case

. We rewrite the configuration reached
after
n
steps as follows:

{(\langle{\text{{*}}\mathtt{E}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\mathtt{F}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,b\rangle:F,{({\mu},w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}})},b_{\!\mathit{ms}})\mathrel{:}S^{\prime\prime}}

By the IH, we know that this configuration satisfies the predicate
\mathsf{wf}
. The target configuration after the transition takes the form:

{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,b\rangle:F,{({[\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}^{\mathsf{Addr}}\mapsto\llbracket\mathtt{F}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}]}\mathrel{:}{\mu},w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}})},b_{\!\mathit{ms}})\mathrel{:}S^{\prime\prime}}.

From the premises of the rule, we have
\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}^{\mathsf{Addr}}\in\underline{w}(\mathsf{ArrId}_{b})
. The remaining conditions required to establish
\mathsf{wf}
follow directly from the IH.

-

Case

. The configuration reached after
n
steps rewrites as follows:

{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{call}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\mathtt{E}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{E}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,b\rangle:F,{({\mu},w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}})},b_{\!\mathit{ms}})\mathrel{:}S^{\prime\prime}}.

According to the IH, this configuration satisfies
\mathsf{wf}
. The
target configuration after the call looks as follows:

(\langle w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}}(p),\rho^{\prime},b\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,b\rangle:F,{({\mu},w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}})},b_{\!\mathit{ms}})\mathrel{:}S^{\prime\prime}

for some
\rho^{\prime}
and with

p=\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}^{\mathsf{Addr}}
. From the rule’s
premises, we know
p\in\underline{w}(\mathsf{ProcId}_{b})
, indicating
the existence of a function
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}}\in\mathsf{ProcId}_{b}
such that

w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})=p
. Using the definition of
\cdot\mathrel{\diamond}\cdot
, we
obtain
w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}}(p)={\tau^{\prime}}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})=\tau({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})
, where
the last equation is a consequence of the IH. Next, we analyze the
cases based on
b
. If
b=\mathtt{u}
, the function body is
unprivileged, which proves
\mathtt{u}(w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}}(p))
, as
required. If
b=\mathtt{k}
, we observe that

w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}}(p)\in\mathtt{Cmd}
, thus showing

\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}(w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}}(p))
, as needed. The remaining
conditions follow directly from the IH.

-

Case

. We begin by applying the IH, which establishes that the configuration reached after
n
steps satisfies
\mathsf{wf}
:

\sigma\vdash\mathsf{wf}_{w}((\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{E}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{E}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,b\rangle:F,{({\mu}^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}})},b_{\!\mathit{ms}})\mathrel{:}S^{\prime\prime}).

The proof proceeds by case analysis on
b
.

-

Case

b=\mathtt{u}
. From the IH we have:

\mathtt{u}({\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{E}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{E}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F}).

The target configuration takes the form:

{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle\mathrel{:}\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle\mathrel{:}F,{({\mu}^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}})},b_{\!\mathit{ms}})\mathrel{:}S^{\prime\prime}}.

for some
\rho^{\prime}
. To complete the proof, it suffices to observe that
\mathtt{k}(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle)
, which follows from the definition of
\gamma
.

-

Case

b=\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}
. By the IH, we know that
\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{E}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{E}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}\rangle\mathrel{:}F=\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}\rangle\mathrel{:}\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}\rangle\mathrel{:}F_{\mathtt{k}}\mathrel{:}F_{\mathtt{u}}
with and
\mathtt{u}(F_{\mathtt{u}})
and
\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}(F_{\mathtt{k}})
. The target configuration is:

{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}\rangle\mathrel{:}\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}\rangle\mathrel{:}F_{\mathtt{k}}\mathrel{:}F_{\mathtt{u}},{({\mu}^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau^{\prime}})},b_{\!\mathit{ms}})\mathrel{:}S^{\prime\prime}}.

Observe that
\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho^{\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}\rangle\mathrel{:}\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{E}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{E}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}\rangle\mathrel{:}F_{\mathtt{k}})
holds, establishing the claim.

∎

Remark 11
.

For every system
\sigma=(\tau,\gamma,\xi)
, every store
\tau=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau^{\prime}
, program configuration
\phi={(F_{\mathtt{k}}:F_{\mathtt{u}},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}
where
\mathtt{k}(F_{\mathtt{k}})
and
\mathtt{u}(F_{\mathtt{u}})
, and configuration
{(F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime})}
that is reachable in
n
steps from
\phi
, there exist a pair of stacks
F_{\mathtt{k}}^{\prime},F_{\mathtt{u}}^{\prime}
such that
F^{\prime}=F_{\mathtt{k}}^{\prime}:F_{\mathtt{u}}^{\prime}
, and
\mathtt{k}(F_{\mathtt{k}}^{\prime})
and
\mathtt{u}(F_{\mathtt{u}}^{\prime})
hold.

Proof.

We prove this by induction on the number of steps,
n
.

-

Case
0. The base case is trivial.

-

Case

n+1
. The proof proceeds by cases on the rule applied to establish the last transition. Most rules are straightforward, so we focus on the more interesting cases:

-

Case

. The target configuration contains a stack that is a suffix of the stack in the source configuration. Hence, the conclusion follows trivially from the IH.

-

Case

. In this case, we first apply the IH, which shows:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(F_{\mathtt{k}}:F_{\mathtt{u}},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to^{n}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{E}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{E}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho^{\prime},b\rangle\mathrel{:}F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}

and that the stack of frames
\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{E}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{E}_{k}),\rho^{\prime},b\rangle\mathrel{:}F^{\prime}
is a concatenation of a pair of stacks
F_{\mathtt{k}}^{\prime},F_{\mathtt{u}}^{\prime}
such that
\mathtt{k}(F_{\mathtt{k}}^{\prime})
and
\mathtt{u}(F_{\mathtt{u}}^{\prime})
hold. Now, consider the next transition:

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{syscall}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}(\mathtt{E}_{1},\dots,\mathtt{E}_{k}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho^{\prime},b\rangle\mathrel{:}F_{\mathtt{k}}^{\prime}\mathrel{:}F_{\mathtt{u}}^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to{{(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho^{\prime\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}\rangle:\langle\mathtt{D},\rho^{\prime},b\rangle\mathrel{:}F_{\mathtt{k}}^{\prime}\mathrel{:}F_{\mathtt{u}}^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}}

for an appropriate
\rho^{\prime\prime}
. The claim requires verifying that the target configuration satisfies the desired properties. In particular, if
b=\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}}
, then
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{t}}}={\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}
, and
\mathtt{k}(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho^{\prime\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle\mathrel{:}\langle\mathtt{D},\rho^{\prime},b\rangle\mathrel{:}F_{\mathtt{k}}^{\prime})
holds trivially by our case analysis rule
. Otherwise, if
b=\mathtt{u}
, then
F_{\mathtt{k}}^{\prime}=\epsilon
by the IH, and we simply need to observe that
\mathtt{k}(\langle\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}),\rho^{\prime\prime},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle)
holds.

-

Case

. This case is analogous to the previous one. Instead of setting the flag to
\mathtt{k}
in the new frame, the rule copies it from the topmost frame of the source configuration, which does not invalidate the invariant. The target configuration looks as follows:

\langle\langle w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime}(p),\rho_{0}[x_{1}\leftarrow\llbracket\mathtt{F}_{1}\rrbracket_{\rho,w},\dots,x_{n}\leftarrow\llbracket\mathtt{F}_{n}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}],b\rangle:\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime}\rangle.

From
Remark

10
, we deduce that
\tau^{\prime\prime}=_{\mathsf{ProcId}}\tau
. Therefore, we have
w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime}(p)
, because from the premises of the rule, we know that
p\in\underline{w}(\mathsf{ProcId}_{b})
. This implies that there exists a function
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}}\in\mathsf{ProcId}_{b}
such that
w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})=p
. Using this observation and the definition of
\cdot\mathrel{\diamond}\cdot
, we deduce that
w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime}(p)=\tau({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})
. Now, we proceed by cases on
b
. If
b=\mathtt{u}
, the body of the function is unprivileged, and this shows that
\mathtt{u}(w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime}(p))
holds. If
b=\mathtt{k}
, we observe that the program is in
\mathtt{Cmd}
, which shows that
\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}(w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime\prime}(p))
holds, as required.

∎

Lemma 16
.

be defined on frame stacks as follows:

\displaystyle\mathsf{hasu}(\epsilon)

\displaystyle\triangleq\bot

\displaystyle\mathsf{hasu}(f\mathrel{:}F)

and on configuration stacks as follows:

\displaystyle\mathsf{hasu}(\epsilon)

\displaystyle\triangleq\top

.

Proof.

The proof proceeds by induction. The base case is trivial. In the inductive step, we perform a case analysis on the directive used for the last transition:

-

Case

\mathsf{st}
. By inspecting this fragment of the semantics, we deduce that the
n
-th and the
n+1
-th target configurations have the same number of configurations. Therefore, the
n
-th target stack must contain exactly one configuration. As a result, we can apply the IH and deduce that the mis-speculation flag of the
n
-th target configuration is
\bot
. Furthermore, we observe that for all the rules producing a transition with the
\mathsf{st}
directive, the flag of the source configuration and the target configuration remains the same. Hence, we conclude the proof for this case.

-

Case

\mathsf{ld}\,i,\mathsf{br}\,b,\mathsf{run}\,p
. For all the rules that match these directives, the claim holds due to the vacuity of the premise: the
n+1
-th target configuration stack has a height greater than
1
. The only exception is
. In this case, the proof follows the same reasoning as the case where the rule uses the
\mathsf{st}
directive, which has already been considered in the previous step.

-

Case

{\mathsf{bt}}
. We go by case analysis on the applied rule, which must be one of
or
.

-

Case

. In this case, the claim follows directly from the definition of the rule.

-

Case

. Let
S_{n}
denote the
n
-th target configuration stack. Note that its height can neither be
0
nor
1
. In the first case, there would be no subsequent transition, while in the second case, applying the IH would imply that the mis-speculation flag is
\bot
, contradicting the assumption about the applied rule.
If the height of
S_{n}
is greater than
2
, then the height of the
n+1
-th target stack is greater than
1
, so the claim holds due to the vacuity of the premise.
Finally, if the height is exactly
2
, then
S_{n}
must have the shape
\chi_{n}\mathrel{:}\chi_{n}^{\prime}
. By
Remark

17
, we know that there is a sequence of transitions from
\phi
to
\chi_{n}^{\prime}
of length
n^{\prime}\leq n
. By applying the IH to this sequence, we can show that
\chi_{n}^{\prime}
has the mis-speculation flag unset. We conclude by noting that the
n+1
-th target configuration stack is precisely
\chi_{n}^{\prime}
.

∎

Otherwise, the applied rule is
. We go by case analysis on the height of the configuration stack

. By introspection of the rule and the main assumption of this claim, we deduce that the mis-speculation flag of

\bot

17
to the

\phi

The following lemma establishes that the output of a
system-call semantics
preserving
transformation remains semantically equivalent to its input.

Lemma 20
.

Let
\sigma=({\tau}_{1},\gamma_{1},\xi_{1})
be a system, and let

\zeta(\sigma)=({\tau}_{2},\gamma_{2},\xi_{2})
.
If
\zeta
is
system-call semantics preserving
, then the systems

\sigma
and
\zeta(\sigma)
are
semantically equivalent
.

Proof.

To establish the main claim, we first prove the following auxiliary claim.
Let

\phi_{1}={(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau}_{1})}\quad\text{and}\quad\phi_{2}={(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle,w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau}_{2})}.

and every pair of systems

\sigma_{1}
and
\sigma_{2}
whose system calls have the same semantics
in the sense of
Definition

6

w\vdash_{\sigma_{1}}\phi_{1}\to^{n}{(F,w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau}_{1}^{\prime})}\land\mathtt{u}(F_{1})\Rightarrow w\vdash_{\sigma_{2}}\phi_{2}\to^{*}{(F,w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau}_{2}^{\prime})}\land{\tau}_{1}^{\prime}=_{\mathsf{Id}_{\mathtt{u}}\cup\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{k}}}{\tau}_{2}^{\prime}.

A.3.2
Technical Observations on the
\eta
Transformation

We say that two programs
\mathtt{C},\mathtt{C}^{\prime}
are in relation
\mathtt{C}\precsim\mathtt{C}^{\prime}
if and only if

\mathtt{C}^{\prime}
can be obtained by substituting instructions
{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{call}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\mathtt{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathtt{F}_{k})
with
{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{scall}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\mathtt{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathtt{F}_{k})
and by placing
{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{fence}}}
instruction inside
\mathtt{C}
.

We extend this relation to configurations by stipulating

\epsilon\precsim\epsilon\quad\tau\precsim\tau^{\prime}\lx@proof@logical@and\tau=_{\mathsf{Id}_{\mathtt{u}}\cup\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{k}}}\tau^{\prime}\forall{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}}\in\mathsf{ProcId}_{\mathtt{k}}.\tau^{\prime}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})\precsim(\tau({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}}))\quad\gamma\precsim\gamma^{\prime}\forall{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}\in\mathsf{Sys}.\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}})\precsim\gamma({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}})^{\prime}\quad(\tau,\gamma,\xi)\precsim(\tau^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime},\xi)\lx@proof@logical@and\tau\precsim\tau^{\prime}\gamma\precsim\gamma^{\prime}

\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:F\precsim\langle\mathtt{C}^{\prime},\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:F^{\prime}\lx@proof@logical@and F\precsim F^{\prime}\mathtt{C}\precsim\mathtt{C}^{\prime}\quad\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F\precsim\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime}F\precsim F^{\prime}

\mathsf{err}\precsim\mathsf{err}\quad\mathsf{unsafe}\precsim\mathsf{unsafe}\quad{(F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\precsim{(F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\lx@proof@logical@and\tau\precsim\tau^{\prime}F\precsim F^{\prime}

Lemma 21
.

For every pair of systems
\sigma\precsim\sigma^{\prime}
, and for any configurations

\phi={(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}

and

\chi
such that
\phi\precsim\chi
, if

w\vdash_{\sigma}\phi\to\phi^{\prime},

then there exists a configuration
\chi^{\prime}
such that

w\vdash_{\sigma^{\prime}}\chi\to^{*}\chi^{\prime},

and
\phi^{\prime}\precsim\chi^{\prime}
.

Proof.

We rewrite the configurations
\phi,\chi
as follows:

\phi={(\langle\mathtt{C},\rho,b\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}

and

\chi={(\langle\mathtt{C}^{\prime},\rho,b\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}.

with

and
\tau\precsim\tau^{\prime}
. We proceed by cases on

.

-

\mathtt{u}
.
The proof goes by cases on the rule that has been applied to
\mathtt{C}
. We show some of the most relevant cases.
In all of the cases within this sub-derivation, we have

by the assumption

.

-

Case

.
The assumption is

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle x\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}\mathtt{E}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to\\
{{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{x}\leftarrow{\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}}.

By applying the same rule to
\chi
, we obtain:

w\vdash_{\sigma^{\prime}}{(\langle x\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}\mathtt{E}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to\\
{{(\langle\mathtt{D},{\rho[{x}\leftarrow{\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}}]},\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}}

which establishes the claim.

-

Case

.
The assumption is

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\text{{*}}\mathtt{E}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\mathtt{F}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to\\
{{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F,{w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau}[{p}\leftarrow{v}]})}},

where
v=\llbracket\mathtt{F}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}
and
p=\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}^{\mathsf{Addr}}
.
Observe that
p\in\underline{w}(\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{u}})
, meaning that there exists a pair
({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}},i)
such that
w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}})+i=p
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}}\in\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{u}}
.
Thus, we have that

{w\mathrel{\diamond}{\tau}[{p}\leftarrow{v}]}={w\mathrel{\diamond}{{{\tau}[{({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}},i)}\leftarrow{v}]}}}

due to
Remark

4
.
Applying the same rule to
\chi
, we obtain:

w\vdash_{\sigma^{\prime}}{(\langle{\text{{*}}\mathtt{E}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\mathtt{F}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to\\
{{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}{{{\tau^{\prime}}[{({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}},i)}\leftarrow{v}]}})}},

and to complete the proof, we observe that
{{\tau}[{({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}},i)}\leftarrow{v}]}\precsim{{\tau^{\prime}}[{({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}},i)}\leftarrow{v}]}
, which follows from the assumption
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{a}}}\in\mathsf{ArrId}_{\mathtt{u}}
.

Case

The assumption is

w\vdash_{\sigma}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{call}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\vec{\mathtt{F}}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)}\to\\
{(\langle w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau(\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}^{\mathsf{Addr}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{u}\rangle:{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F,w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)})},

where
\rho_{0}^{\prime}
is a shorthand for
\rho_{0}[\vec{x}\leftarrow\llbracket\vec{\mathtt{F}}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}]
. From the premise of the rule, we infer that there exists
{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}}\in\mathsf{ProcId}_{\mathtt{u}}
such that

\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}^{\mathsf{Addr}}=w({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})

Thus, from the definition of
w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau
and the definition of the
\precsim
relation, we deduce that

w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau=\tau({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})=\tau^{\prime}({\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{f}}})
,
where
\tau^{\prime}
is the store of (‡). Consequently, these observations allow us to demonstrate that applying the same rule to

w\vdash_{\sigma^{\prime}}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{call}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\vec{\mathtt{F}}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to\\
{{(\langle w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau(\llbracket\mathtt{E}\rrbracket_{\rho,w}^{\mathsf{Addr}}),\rho_{0}^{\prime},\mathtt{u}\rangle:{(\langle\mathtt{D},\rho,\mathtt{u}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})})}},

thereby proving the claim.

Case

Under this assumption, most cases are analogous to the corresponding ones for user-mode execution. Similarly, we proceed by case analysis on the rule that establishes the transition, focusing on the most significant cases.

-

Case

.
The assumption is

From the assumption on the initial configurations, the configuration
\chi
in (†) has the form

\displaystyle x\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}\mathtt{E}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{fence}}}{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D}^{\prime}

for

The claim follows from the observation that

In the third case, we observe that:

w\vdash_{\sigma^{\prime}}{(\langle{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{call}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\vec{\mathtt{F}}){\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{;\,}}}\mathtt{D}^{\prime},\rho,\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle:F^{\prime},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau^{\prime})}\to^{*}\\

Corollary 1
.

For every two systems

\sigma=({\tau}_{1},\gamma_{1},\xi)\precsim({\tau}_{2},\gamma_{2},\xi)=\sigma^{\prime}
,
every layout
w
, unprivileged command
\mathtt{C}
, and registers
\rho
, we have

\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma,w}(\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{u},{\tau}_{1})\simeq\mathit{Eval}_{\sigma^{\prime},w}(\mathtt{C},\rho,\mathtt{u},{\tau}_{2}),

where the equivalence is that of
Definition

6
, i.e.,

(v,\tau_{1})\simeq(v,\tau_{2})
if

\tau_{1}=_{\mathsf{Id}_{\mathtt{u}}}\tau_{2}
, and it coincides with equality otherwise.

Proof.

Observe that the initial configurations are in
\precsim
relation, therefore the claim
is a trivial consequence of
Lemma

21
.
∎

Corollary 2
.

Transformations
\eta,{\psi},\theta

preserve the semantics of the systems.

Proof.

Observe that for any
\zeta\in\{\eta,{\psi},\theta\}
,
we always have
\sigma\precsim\zeta(\sigma)
. Hence, the conclusion
follows as a trivial consequence of
Corollary

1
.
∎

\mathtt{Q}_{1},\ldots,\mathtt{Q}_{h}
such that for every
1\leq i\leq h
, it holds that

\mathtt{Q}_{i}={\psi^{\top}_{\bot}}(\mathtt{C}_{i}).

We proceed by cases on
\vec{\mathtt{Q}}
:

-

Case

\vec{\mathtt{Q}}=\varepsilon
. The proof proceeds by cases on
\mathtt{C}

-

Case

\mathtt{C}=\varepsilon
.
In this case, from (H3) and by analyzing the applicable rules, we deduce that the only directive compatible with this command is
\mathsf{st}
, and that the transition rule applied must be
. Furthermore, by inspecting this rule, we conclude that
F
is not empty. Consequently, from (H2), we derive that

F={\langle{\psi^{\top}_{\bot}}(\mathtt{C}_{1}),\rho_{1},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle\mathrel{:}\ldots\mathrel{:}\langle{\psi^{\top}_{\bot}}(\mathtt{C}_{k}),\rho_{k},\mathtt{k}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0547,0.4414,0.3477}{\mathtt{s}}}}\rangle}
.
Thus, the only reachable stack of configurations is

(F,{({\mu},w\mathrel{\diamond}\tau)},b_{\!\mathit{ms}})\mathrel{:}S.

We include this configuration in
Z
, while the other elements of
Z
are not relevant for this part of the proof and can be instantiated with any suitable values.
This stack satisfies conditions (C1), (C2), and (C3A).
Claim (C1) holds because, by analyzing the definition of
{\psi^{\top}_{\bot}}(\cdot)
, we deduce that
{\psi^{\top}_{\bot}}(\mathtt{C}_{1})
cannot be a member of the set
\{x\ \mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}\text{{*}}{\mathtt{E}},{\text{{*}}\mathtt{E}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\mathtt{F}},{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{scall}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\vec{\mathtt{F}})\}
. Claim (C2) follows from (H2).

Case

\mathtt{C}=\mathtt{I};\mathtt{D}
. The proof proceeds by case analysis on the instruction
\mathtt{I}
.

-

Case

\mathtt{I}={\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{skip}}}

\mathsf{st}

. In addition, the resulting configuration stack is

To establish (C1), we proceed by case analysis on the value of

{\psi^{\top}_{e}}(\cdot)

{\psi^{m}_{e}}(\mathtt{D})
cannot belong to the set
\{x\ \mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}\text{{*}}{\mathtt{E}},{\text{{*}}\mathtt{E}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{{:}{=}}}}}{\mathtt{F}},{\color[rgb]{0.0273,0.2383,0.4336}{\mathtt{scall}}}\ \mathtt{E}(\vec{\mathtt{F}})\}

Finally, claim (C2) follows directly from (H2), since this transition does not alter the state.

Depending on the applied rule, the target configuration can be one of the following:

Appendix B
Discussion on SESES Performance Evaluation

In
Section

7
, we observe that SESES alone is insufficient to prevent the speculative attacks we consider there. However, we also note that combining SESES with the
lvi-cfi
pass and a BTB mitigation technique, such as retpoline or eIBRS, could prevent those attacks. Since SESES is not compatible with retpoline, we attempted to evaluate a configuration with SESES and eIBRS.

We made considerable efforts to measure the overhead of SESES under this configuration. Unfortunately, we encountered previously undocumented link-time bugs in
lvi-cfi
that prevented successful compilation of the Linux kernel.

To estimate the potential overhead of SESES and
lvi-cfi
, we analyzed the output of the aborted compilation. Specifically, we counted the number of
lfence
instructions in the
vmlinux.o
file and compared it to the counts resulting from our own transformations. The results are shown in the following table:

Simple Fencing

Transformation

Optimized fencing

Transformation

Non-speculating

Transformation

SESES +
lvi-cfi

1083\cdot 10^{3}

530\cdot 10^{3}

1045\cdot 10^{3}

1123\cdot 10^{3}

Table 7
:
Count of
lfence
instructions for different transformations.

While this analysis does not provide runtime overhead measurements, it
supports the hypothesis that the performance cost of SESES combined
with
lvi-cfi
would be similar to that of our Simple Fencing
Transformation.
